title: Why Do We Need Warm-up? A Theoretical Perspective
claim: Local curvature scales roughly linearly with loss suboptimality during early training, consistently across model sizes.
layout: 3 scatter panels in a row, each with a training-progress colorbar and dashed fit
description: Three side-by-side scatter plots, one per language model size (70M, 160M, 410M on FineWeb). In each, the x-axis is training loss (about 9.5 to 11) and the y-axis is estimated local smoothness (scaled by 10^4). Dense dots form a smooth curve, colored by iteration with a plasma colormap. Dark purple marks early training and yellow marks later training, and a colorbar sits at the right of each panel. A black dashed line gives the best linear fit. The points follow this line closely through the middle of the curve. They flatten or bend away at the highest-loss start, where training begins, and they flatten at the low-loss end. Panel titles sit below as text. The eye goes first to the colored curve hugging the dashed line.
caption: Local smoothness approximation versus training loss for language models of varying sizes on the FineWeb dataset, using SGD with gradient clipping 1 with a constant LR of 10−4. Each dot represents estimated local smoothness and stochastic training loss, with color indicating training progress, while the black dashed line shows the best linear fit. For much of early training, the relation is well-approximated by a line.
abstract: Learning rate warm-up -- increasing the learning rate at the beginning of training -- has become a ubiquitous heuristic in modern deep learning, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a principled explanation for why warm-up improves training. We rely on a generalization of the $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness condition, which bounds local curvature as a linear function of the loss suboptimality and exhibits desirable closure properties. We show -- both theoretically and empirically -- that this condition is satisfied by common neural architectures and accurately captures the curvature of the optimization landscape early in training. Adapting the learning rate in response to this curvature condition naturally induces a warm-up-like schedule, and we show that this choice yields provably faster convergence guarantees than using a fixed learning rate. Experiments on language and vision models show that the resulting one-parameter warm-up schedule can match tuned linear warm-up and improve over no warm-up.
